text: Penguins are birds that gave up flying in air to fly underwater. Most cruise at about 5 to 10 km/h, roughly a brisk walking or jogging pace. But in short bursts, the gentoo penguin can reach about 36 km/h, the fastest of any penguin.

That's about four times faster than the best human [[@swimming|swimmers]], who top out at roughly 8 to 9 km/h in a race. A penguin uses its wings as stiff flippers, flapping them up and down so they push water on both strokes. Its body is shaped like a torpedo, and its feet and tail steer like a rudder.

myth: Penguins live at both the North and South Poles.

Wild penguins live only in the Southern Hemisphere, from Antarctica to South Africa, Australia and South America. The one exception, the Galápagos penguin, lives right on the equator and sometimes crosses just north of it. There are no wild penguins in the Arctic.

sec.t:
On land, a penguin looks a little silly. In water, everything about it makes sense. Its short, stiff wings have flattened bones fused into a paddle. Its bones are dense rather than hollow, so it doesn't bob up like a cork. Short, tightly packed feathers form a smooth, waterproof coat.

Even the black-and-white colours help. From below, a penguin's white belly blends with the bright sky. From above, its black back blends with the dark water. This trick, called countershading, hides it from both hunters and prey. Some penguins also "porpoise", leaping out of the water as they swim, because moving through air for a moment takes less effort than pushing through water.

Emperor penguins have a special trick for getting out of the water. Before they leap onto the ice, they fluff their feathers to trap air, then dive. As they shoot back up, they release the air as a coat of tiny bubbles.

A 2011 study found that this bubble coat reduces drag, the water's resistance, and lets them roughly double their speed for a few seconds. They burst out of the water and land on the ice edge, sometimes a metre or more above the surface. Engineers are interested in using bubble coats to help ships move with less fuel.

Many people picture penguins only on Antarctic ice. In fact, of about 18 species, only a few live on [[@antarctica|Antarctica]] itself. Others live on rocky coasts and islands in South America, South Africa, Australia and New Zealand. The African penguin nests on beaches near Cape Town, and the Galápagos penguin lives right on the equator.

Their speed matters, because they're both hunters and hunted. Penguins chase fish, squid and krill, and leopard seals, sea lions and orcas chase them. To survive, they need to be quick and to turn sharply, darting sideways to dodge a seal's jaws.

Humans have borrowed from penguins too. Swimsuit designers study smooth, streamlined bodies to cut drag, and some suits got so good at it that swimming's rule makers banned the fastest full-body ones in 2010. Sport is full of such arguments about gear, from swimsuits to the springy soles of racing [[@sport-science-shoes|sports shoes]].

text: Plastic reaches the ocean from rivers, beaches, drains, ships and [[@fishing-boats|fishing boats]]. Once in the sea, it goes several places. Some floats and is carried by [[@ocean-currents|ocean currents]] into slow, swirling areas called gyres, where it collects in patches. Some washes back onto beaches. Much of it sinks to the sea floor, even into the deepest trenches.

Plastic does not rot like food or leaves. Instead, sunlight and waves slowly break it into smaller and smaller pieces. Bits smaller than 5 mm are called [[microplastic|microplastics]]. They are now found almost everywhere scientists look, from Arctic ice to deep-sea mud, and inside fish, birds and other animals.

st.reveal: Floating patches get the most attention, but they hold only a small share. Much plastic sinks, settles on the seabed, washes up on shores or breaks into pieces too small to see. Plastic doesn't dissolve; it just gets smaller.

sec.t:
Ocean currents move in giant loops. In the middle of each loop, the water turns slowly and floating things gather there. The biggest of these areas is the Great Pacific Garbage Patch, between Hawaii and California.

A 2018 study estimated the patch covers about 1.6 million square km, more than twice the size of Texas, or roughly half the size of India. But it is not a floating island. Most of it is scattered bits of plastic, often tiny, mixed through the top layer of water. By weight, a large share is old fishing nets and ropes. Similar patches exist in the Atlantic and Indian Oceans.

Sea animals often mistake plastic for food. [[@sea-turtles|Sea turtles]] swallow plastic bags that [[@jellyfish-sting|drift like jellyfish]], one of their favourite meals. Seabirds such as albatrosses pick up bright bits of plastic floating on the water and feed them to their chicks. On Midway Atoll, in the middle of the Pacific, dead albatross chicks have been found with stomachs full of [[@water-bottle|bottle caps]] and lighters.

Seals, dolphins and whales can get tangled in lost fishing nets, which keep drifting and trapping animals for years. Scientists call these "ghost nets". Scientists are also studying how microplastics affect smaller animals, and people who eat seafood, but those effects are still not well understood.

The best way to keep plastic out of the sea is to stop it getting there. That means using less, collecting waste properly and [[@recycling|recycling]] more. India banned many single-use plastic items, such as plastic cutlery, straws and some thin bags, from July 2022. Several US states, starting with California, have banned thin plastic shopping bags.

[[@beach-clean|People clean up too]]. From 2015, a lawyer named Afroz Shah and [[@volunteering|volunteers]] began clearing tonnes of rubbish from Versova Beach in [[@mumbai|Mumbai]], week after week. In 2018, olive ridley turtles were seen hatching on the cleaned beach. The [[@united-nations|United Nations]] gave him its Champions of the Earth award, and his story is one of many in [[@environment-heroes|environment heroes]].

text: Deer and many other prey animals have eyes with only two kinds of colour detectors. Orange and green look similar to them.
Stripes break up the tiger's outline in tall grass and shadows. That's [[@camouflage|camouflage]].
Every tiger's stripes are different, like [[@fingerprints|fingerprints]]. Scientists count tigers from camera-trap photos this way.

So the tiger's coat isn't really designed for our eyes. To a chital or a sambar deer, a tiger crouching in dry grass is a dull greenish shape broken into stripy pieces. By the time the deer spots it, the tiger may already be springing.

myth: White tigers are albinos, or a separate kind of tiger.

White tigers are Bengal tigers with a rare gene that stops orange colour forming. Unlike albinos, they still have dark stripes and usually blue eyes. They are very rare in the wild, and almost all live in zoos.

sec.t:
Our eyes have three kinds of colour cells; a deer's have two.

People with normal vision have cone cells that respond to red, green and blue light. Deer lack the red-sensitive kind, so reds and oranges blend with greens, a little like a person with red-green [[@colour-blindness|colour blindness]]. In 2019, scientists at the University of Bristol modelled how a tiger looks through a deer's eyes. To the deer, the orange tiger was almost as well hidden as a green one would be.

A tiger's stripes aren't only in its fur. Shave a patch, and the [[@skin|skin]] underneath is striped too, because the colour comes from the skin cells that grow each hair. Most tigers have over 100 stripes, and no two tigers share the same pattern. Even a tiger's left and right sides are different.

Camera traps take photos when a tiger walks past. [[@ai-what|Computer programs]] compare stripe patterns to tell tigers apart and count them.

Every four years, India runs one of the biggest wildlife surveys in the world. In the 2022 count, forest staff set up camera traps at tens of thousands of spots and collected millions of photos. They identified over 3,000 individual tigers and estimated about 3,682 in total.

India started Project Tiger in 1973 to protect tigers and their forests. Today there are over 50 tiger reserves.

It began with nine reserves, including Corbett in Uttarakhand, Kanha in Madhya Pradesh and the [[@sundarbans-tigers|Sundarbans]] in West Bengal. In the early 1970s, only about 1,800 tigers were counted in India, though methods then were rough. Protecting tigers also protects the rivers and forests they need, along with the deer, birds and plants that share them. That's why the tiger, India's [[@national-symbols|national animal]], is often called an umbrella species.

Once in a while, a Bengal tiger is born white. In 1951, a white cub named Mohan was captured in the forests of Rewa, in present-day Madhya Pradesh. He was kept by the Maharaja of Rewa, and many white tigers in zoos around the world descend from him.

text: Cities are full of wild animals. Pigeons, crows, sparrows and [[@squirrels|squirrels]] are easy to spot. Cities offer food, water, warm buildings to shelter in and, in many places, fewer large predators. Some animals manage well among people and traffic. Others struggle with roads, glass windows, bright lights and noise. Scientists study city wildlife to learn how animals adapt and how cities can share space with them.

sec.t:
Sanjay Gandhi National Park covers about 100 square kilometres of forested hills in the north of [[@mumbai|Mumbai]], surrounded by tower blocks and busy roads. It is home to [[@leopards-cities|dozens of leopards]], along with spotted deer, monkeys, pythons and more than 250 kinds of birds.

Leopards mostly hunt at night and sometimes wander into nearby housing colonies, where stray dogs are easy prey. Forest officials, scientists and local residents have worked together on campaigns teaching people how to stay safe, such as keeping rubbish cleared and walking in groups after dark.

In Delhi, thousands of black [[@kites-birds|kites]] circle in the sky. They feed on scraps from markets and rubbish, and in some neighbourhoods, people throw meat to them as a traditional act of charity. Brothers in Delhi who have spent years rescuing injured kites were the subject of an award-winning documentary in 2022.

Near Mumbai, tens of thousands of [[@flamingos-pink|flamingos]] spend the winter on the mudflats of Thane Creek, feeding beside factories and flyovers. In New York and Chicago, peregrine falcons nest on tall buildings and bridges, diving on pigeons from high ledges as if from cliffs.

In Austin, Texas, about 1.5 million Mexican free-tailed bats roost under the Congress Avenue Bridge in summer. At sunset they stream out in long ribbons to hunt insects, and crowds gather on the bridge to watch.

In Chicago, scientists have tracked coyotes that live among car parks and railways, mostly unseen. Raccoons in many North American cities open bins and even learn to open doors. In Indian towns, rhesus macaques and langurs leap across rooftops. Some animals are good at city life, and people are still learning how to live alongside them.

City planners now think about animals as well as people. Green roofs, tree-lined streets and parks joined by leafy strips give birds and insects places to feed and travel. Some cities dim their lights during bird migration seasons, because bright windows confuse birds flying at night. In Bengaluru and other Indian cities, volunteers have helped clean and restore old lakes, which bring back herons, kingfishers and dragonflies. Good [[@urban-planning|urban planning]] can make a city better for its wild neighbours and its people at the same time.

text: Most car engines are internal combustion engines, which means the fuel burns inside the engine itself. The engine has several metal tubes called cylinders. Inside each one, a tightly fitting piston slides up and down.

A tiny mist of petrol mixed with air is let into a cylinder. The piston squeezes it, and a spark plug lights it. The fuel burns in a flash, the hot gases expand and they shove the piston down hard. Each piston is joined to a crankshaft, a bent metal rod that turns the up-and-down push into spinning, a bit like your legs pushing [[@bicycle-balance|bicycle]] pedals round. Through gears, that spin turns the wheels.
A four-cylinder engine at ordinary speed fires its cylinders thousands of times every minute.

st.reveal: Squeezing air makes it hotter. A diesel engine crushes air into a very small space, heating it to several hundred degrees. When diesel fuel is sprayed in, it catches fire instantly. That's why diesel engines are built extra strong and sound so knocky.

d.try: Act out the four strokes with three friends. One person is the piston going down and drawing in air (suck), the next moves up to squeeze it (squeeze), the third claps for the spark and jumps down (bang), and the fourth pushes upwards to clear the exhaust (blow). Repeat the cycle faster and faster to feel how an engine speeds up.
myth: Petrol explodes inside a car engine.

The fuel and air burn extremely fast, but in a controlled way that spreads smoothly through the cylinder. A true explosion would damage the engine. When fuel does go off too suddenly, mechanics call it knocking, and engines are designed to prevent it.

sec.t:
Each cylinder goes through four steps, called strokes, over and over.

First comes **intake**. The piston slides down and a valve opens, drawing in air and fuel. Mechanics call this "suck". Then **compression**: the valves close and the piston moves up, squeezing the mixture into a small space. That's "squeeze". Next comes **power**. The spark plug fires, the fuel burns and the expanding gas pushes the piston down. That's "bang". Last is **exhaust**. Another valve opens and the piston moves up, pushing the burnt gases out to the exhaust pipe. That's "blow".

Only the power stroke actually pushes. The spinning crankshaft and the other cylinders carry the piston through the other three.

A car engine is not very efficient. Of all the energy stored in the petrol, only around a quarter actually moves the car. Most of the rest becomes heat. Some leaves through the exhaust, and a lot is carried away by the radiator, which pumps water around the engine to stop it overheating.

Burning petrol and diesel also makes carbon dioxide and other gases. Some of them add to [[@air-pollution|air pollution]] and [[@fog-smog|smog]] in cities like Delhi and Los Angeles. Carbon dioxide adds to [[@climate-change|climate change]]. Catalytic converters in exhaust pipes clean up some of the harmful gases, but they can't remove the carbon dioxide.

Diesel engines, invented by Rudolf Diesel in the 1890s, have no spark plugs. They squeeze air so hard it becomes hot enough to light the fuel the moment it is sprayed in. They use less fuel than petrol engines, which is why most trucks, buses and many trains use them.

Many cities in India run buses and autorickshaws on CNG, compressed natural gas, which burns more cleanly than diesel. Hybrid cars pair an engine with a battery and an electric motor. And [[@electric-cars|electric cars]] skip the burning entirely. Their motors have far fewer moving parts, and no pistons at all.

text: A periscope is a tube with a mirror at each end. The top mirror is tilted at 45 degrees, facing out over the thing you want to see past, such as a wall or a crowd. Light from the scene hits it and bounces straight down the tube. At the bottom, a second mirror, also at 45 degrees, bounces the light out sideways into your eye.
The light has gone down and around a corner, so you can see over things while staying hidden or lower down. Its name comes from Greek words that mean "to look around".
Big periscopes on submarines add lenses and prisms to make a sharper, magnified view.

sec.t:
Light travels in straight lines until it hits something. A smooth, shiny surface like a mirror sends it off again at the same angle it arrived. A mirror tilted at 45 degrees turns a beam of light through a right angle, like a car turning a corner.

Two such mirrors, one above the other, turn the light twice. First it goes down the tube, then out to your eye. Each mirror also reverses the picture once, so after two bounces it's the right way round again. That's why you can read a sign through a periscope.

You don't need to understand it to use it. Your [[@eyes-see|eyes]] just see the light arriving and your brain shows you the world on the other side of the wall.

For most of the 1900s, a [[@submarines|submarine]] under the surface was almost blind. To look around, the captain brought it up to just below the waves and raised a long periscope through the top. It might stick out of the water only a little, hard for an enemy ship to spot.

Submarine periscopes are long, carefully built tubes. Instead of plain mirrors, they use glass prisms that bend light without blurring, and sets of lenses that magnify distant ships. The captain could turn the periscope in a full circle by walking round with it, gripping its handles.

Many modern submarines no longer have a tube you look through. They use a mast fitted with cameras and sensors. It pokes above the water and sends pictures by cable to screens inside, where the whole crew can see them. Because the mast doesn't need to pass straight down into the hull, designers can put the control room wherever they like.

Periscopes haven't disappeared, though. Tanks have small ones so the crew can see out while staying protected. Some people use cardboard ones to see over crowds at [[@parades|parades]] and golf tournaments. Scientists studying nuclear reactors use long periscopes to look inside safely. And building a periscope from a carton and two [[@mirrors|mirrors]] is still one of the best ways to learn how light bounces.

text: A touch lamp has a small circuit inside that constantly measures how much electric charge its metal body can hold. That amount is called [[capacitance|capacitance]]. On its own, the lamp holds a tiny, steady amount.

When you touch the metal, your body becomes part of it. You are a big bag of salty water, which conducts electricity well, so together you and the lamp can hold a bit more charge. The circuit notices the jump, decides someone has touched it, and switches the light on, off or to the next brightness. You don't feel anything, because the electrical signals are far too small.

d.try: Test what a phone's touchscreen can feel. With an adult's permission, tap an app with a fingertip, a knuckle, a fingernail, a pencil eraser, a glove, a metal spoon held in your bare hand and a slice of carrot. Most phone screens use the same trick as a touch lamp, so the results should surprise you.
myth: Touch lamps work by sensing the heat of your hand.

They sense electrical charge, not heat. A warm cup won't switch one on, but a cold metal spoon held in your hand will. That is because your body conducts electricity and heat has nothing to do with it.

sec.t:
Think of capacitance like the size of a bucket for electric charge. A small metal lamp base is a small bucket. Your body, much bigger and full of conducting water, is a much bigger one. Touch the lamp and you join the two buckets together.

The circuit inside keeps pouring tiny amounts of charge in and out, thousands of times a second, and times how long it takes to fill. With a bigger bucket it takes longer. That change in timing is the signal. It's a cousin of [[@static-electricity|static electricity]], the charge that makes balloons stick to walls, only far gentler.

Wool, leather, plastic and wood don't conduct electricity well. They act like a wall between your body and the lamp, so the circuit can't sense the extra capacitance. That's why a touch lamp often ignores you when you wear thick winter gloves. Very thin gloves sometimes work anyway, because the circuit can still sense a hand through a thin enough layer.

Metal is different. A metal spoon or key conducts, so it acts like a longer finger. Even damp [[@skin|skin]] works better than very dry skin, because water helps charge move.

Once you know the idea, you see it all over the place. Most phone and tablet screens use capacitive sensing, with a fine grid of see-through wires that can tell exactly where your finger is. That's why a [[@touchscreens|touchscreen]] ignores a plastic pen but responds to a finger, and why special gloves for phones have threads that conduct electricity.

Lift buttons with no moving parts, the glass buttons on [[@induction-stoves|induction stoves]], and the touch controls on some earphones all work the same way. They're popular because there is nothing to press down or break, and the surface can be wiped clean easily. Many cars use the same idea in door handles that open the locks when you touch them.

People sometimes worry about touching a lamp that is "full of electricity". In a touch lamp, the metal you touch is linked only to the low-power sensing circuit. The mains electricity that powers the bulb is kept safely inside. As with any lamp plugged into the wall, though, never open one up or poke inside, and ask an adult if a lamp behaves strangely.

text: Bidri is a metal craft from Bidar, a town in northern [[@karnataka|Karnataka]]. A craftsman casts an object, such as a box or a vase, from an [[alloy|alloy]] that is mostly zinc with a little copper. He then carves fine grooves into it and hammers in silver wire or thin silver sheet.

The final step is the magic one. The piece is rubbed with a warm paste made from special soil and salts. The grey metal turns a deep, velvety black, but the silver does not. The result is a shining silver pattern on a black background, like moonlight on a dark night.

st.reveal: The paste of fort soil and salt reacts with the zinc alloy and darkens it to a deep black. Silver does not react in the same way, so the pattern shines out against the dark background.

There is no paint. The black is a thin layer formed when the zinc alloy reacts with a paste of special soil and salts, so it is part of the metal's surface.
facts: an alloy of mostly zinc with a little copper
silver wire or sheet hammered into grooves

sec.t:
Bidri takes its name from Bidar. In the 1400s, Bidar became the capital of the Bahmani Sultanate, a kingdom in the Deccan with close links to Persia. Craftsmen, poets and architects came from Persia and Central Asia to work there.

Metalworkers brought skills for inlaying one metal into another. Over time they developed this local style. The flowers, vines and geometric shapes on many Bidri pieces still look a lot like patterns in Persian carpets and tiles. Later rulers in the Deccan, and then the [[@princely-states|Nizams of Hyderabad]], kept the craft going.

First, the zinc alloy is melted and poured into a mould made of clay or sand to form the basic shape. After cooling, the surface is filed smooth. It is then dipped briefly in a solution that darkens it a little, so the craftsman can see his design as he scratches it on with a sharp tool.

Next comes the patient part. Using small chisels and a hammer, he cuts the pattern into the surface. Silver wire or sheet is laid into the grooves and hammered until it locks into place. One vase can take days or even weeks.

There are several styles of inlay. In one, called *tarkashi*, fine silver wire is laid into narrow lines. In another, flat pieces of silver sheet are set into wider areas to form leaves and petals. Some pieces combine both, with raised silver that you can feel under your fingers. A few old pieces also used gold or brass.

{{story:rust}}

When the inlay is done, the piece is buffed and gently warmed. Then the craftsman rubs it with a paste of water, salt and soil. Traditionally, the soil comes from old parts of Bidar Fort that have been shaded from sunlight for a long time.

The salts in the paste react with the zinc in the alloy and form a thin black layer on its surface. Silver reacts differently, so it stays bright. This is a chemical change, rather like [[@rust|rusting]] on iron, but this time the result is beautiful and protective. Finally, the piece is rubbed with oil to deepen the black.

In the past, Bidri was used for hookah bases, betel-leaf boxes, washbasins and trays for wealthy households. Many fine old pieces are now in museums, including the Salar Jung Museum in [[@hyderabad|Hyderabad]] and the Victoria and Albert Museum in London.

Today, craftsmen make jewellery boxes, vases, bangles, buttons and paperweights. The work is slow and the number of skilled families is small, so the craft has had government support. Bidriware has a GI tag, a label that protects the name for objects made in the traditional region.

text: No. The colours themselves are the same everywhere, because light and eyes work the same way for everyone. What people feel about a colour is learned, and it changes from place to place.

In much of India, red is the colour of weddings, festivals and good fortune, while white is often worn in mourning. In much of the USA and Europe, brides wear white and mourners wear black. A colour that means joy in one city can mean grief in another.

A few reactions may be shared more widely. Red catches the eye almost everywhere, which may be one reason so many warning signs and [[@traffic-lights|traffic lights]] use it. Scientists are still arguing about how much of this is nature and how much is culture.

st.reveal: In China, as in much of India, red stands for luck and joy. Brides traditionally wear red, and New Year money comes in red envelopes. White is more often linked with mourning.

sec.h: Red for a bride, white for a bride
sec.t:
In many Hindu weddings, the bride wears a red or deep pink sari or lehenga, and red sindoor in the parting of her hair has long been a sign of marriage. Red is linked with [[@life-superstitions|good luck]], energy and new beginnings. In China too, red is the colour of weddings, and [[@new-year|New Year]] money is given in red envelopes.

[[@life-weddings-world|White wedding dresses]] are newer than many people think. In 1840, Queen Victoria of Britain married in white, and wealthy brides in Britain and America copied her. Over the next hundred years, white became the standard in the West. Before that, many brides simply wore their best dress, whatever its colour, and wore it again afterwards.

sec.h: Colours of grief and of prayer
sec.t:
In many Indian families, white is worn after a death, and widows in some communities traditionally dressed in plain white. In the USA, black is the usual colour at funerals, a custom that came from Europe.

[[@saffron|Saffron]] carries deep meaning in India. Many Hindu and Buddhist monks wear saffron, ochre or maroon robes, linked with giving up worldly things. On India's [[@flags|national flag]], the government describes the saffron band as standing for strength and courage. Green is closely linked with Islam and appears on the flags of many Muslim-majority countries. During [[@holi|Holi]], people throw every colour at once, and nobody worries about what any single one means.

sec.h: Do words shape what we see?
sec.t:
Languages divide the rainbow differently. Russian has two everyday words for blue: *goluboy* for light blue and *siniy* for dark blue. Experiments suggest Russian speakers tell those shades apart slightly faster than English speakers do. Some languages use a single word for both green and blue. The ancient Greek poet Homer described the sea as "wine-dark", which has puzzled readers for centuries.

In 1969, two American researchers, Brent Berlin and Paul Kay, compared colour words in many [[@languages-world|languages]]. They argued that languages add colour words in a fairly regular order, starting with dark and light, then red, then green or yellow. Other researchers have challenged parts of their idea, and the argument still runs.

Whatever language you speak, your [[@eyes-see|eyes]] receive the same light as anyone else's. Your culture decides whether that red means a wedding, a warning or a winning team.

text: Pottery is made from clay, a sticky earth made of very tiny particles of weathered rock. When clay is wet, it is soft and can be shaped. When it dries, it holds that shape. When it is heated to very high temperatures in a [[kiln|kiln]], it turns hard, permanent and waterproof enough to hold food and water.

Potters shape clay in three main ways: pinching it with their fingers, building it up from coils or slabs, or spinning it on a potter's wheel. After shaping, the pot is dried, fired, and often coated with a glassy layer called a [[@art-blue-pottery-jaipur|glaze]].

st.prompt: Why does an unglazed clay matka keep drinking water cool in summer?

options.t: Water seeps through tiny pores and evaporates from the outside, carrying heat away
Clay is naturally cold, like ice
The clay absorbs heat and stores it forever

st.reveal: A matka is fired at a fairly low temperature, so it stays slightly porous. A little water soaks through and evaporates from the surface, and evaporation takes heat with it. The same thing cools you when sweat dries.

d.try: Make a pinch pot. Roll a ball of air-dry clay or playdough the size of an orange, push your thumb into the middle, then pinch and turn it gently to thin the walls. Make a second pot with thick walls and compare them when dry. Which is lighter? Which feels stronger?
myth: You can soak an old broken pot in water and turn it back into soft clay.
Firing changes clay chemically. Heat drives out water locked inside the clay's crystals and fuses the particles together. Fired pottery can break, but it will never soften back into clay.
facts: clay, made of tiny rock particles
about 20,000 years old, Xianrendong Cave, China
invented in Mesopotamia, about 5,500 years ago

sec.t:
Clay forms when rocks are slowly broken down by water and weather over thousands of years, the same process that helps make [[@soil-made|soil]]. Clay particles are so small and flat that hundreds would fit side by side across a single millimetre.

When water gets between these flat particles, they slide over each other like a stack of wet [[@cards-games|playing cards]]. That makes clay soft and stretchy. As it dries, the water leaves, the particles lock together, and the clay stiffens.

The potter's wheel was invented in [[@mesopotamia|Mesopotamia]] about 5,500 years ago. Some historians think it came before wheels were put on carts. A spinning wheel lets a potter make round, even pots quickly. The potter centres the clay, pushes a hole in the middle, then lifts the walls up between the fingers as it turns.

In many [[@villages-india|Indian villages]], potters traditionally used a heavy stone or wooden wheel spun with a stick, which kept turning for a long time once it got going. Electric wheels are common today, but the movements of the hands are much the same.

Pottery breaks easily, but the broken pieces, called sherds, last for thousands of years. That makes pottery one of the most useful finds in [[@archaeology|archaeology]]. Styles changed over time, so a sherd can help date a layer of earth.

The [[@indus-cities|Indus Valley cities]], over 4,000 years ago, made fine red pots painted with black patterns of fish scales, peepal leaves and circles. In China, potters developed porcelain, a white, thin, almost see-through ceramic. It was so prized in Europe that people still call fine plates "china".

In India, the kulhad, a small unglazed cup, is still used for chai in many places. [[@candles|Clay diyas]] are made by the million for Diwali, and the matka keeps water cool in summer. In Khurja in Uttar Pradesh and [[@blue-pottery|Blue Pottery]] workshops in Jaipur, potters make glazed plates and vases sold across the country.

In the United States, potters of the Pueblo peoples of New Mexico, such as the famous Maria Martinez of San Ildefonso Pueblo, revived a style of shiny black pottery in the 1900s. They shaped their pots by hand from coils, without a wheel, as their ancestors had done.

text: In remote villages, mail is carried by a mix of roads, trains, buses, boats, jeeps and, very often, people on foot. In India, the last stretch is usually handled by a Gramin Dak Sevak. This village postal worker runs a small branch post office and carries letters, parcels, pensions and money orders door to door.

India has about 1.65 lakh post offices, the largest postal network in the world, and nearly 90 per cent of them are in villages (March 2025). Some sit in places so high or so far away that a letter takes days to get there.

st.prompt: India's PIN codes have six digits. What does the very first digit tell a sorting clerk?

options.t: Which large region of India the letter is going to
The exact street of the house
How heavy the letter is

st.reveal: The first digit stands for one of India's postal zones, such as the north or the south. Each digit after that narrows it down, until the last three point to one particular post office.

d.try: Write a short letter or postcard to a grandparent or relative who lives far away, with their full address and PIN code. Before you post it, look up what each part of the PIN code stands for. Ask them to tell you how many days it took to arrive.
myth: Nobody uses the post office any more, because of phones and email.

Letters have fallen, but post offices now carry huge numbers of parcels from online shopping. In villages they are also banks, pension offices and places to send money, often the only ones for many kilometres.
facts: Hikkim, Himachal Pradesh, listed by Guinness at 4,724 m
Supai, Arizona, in the Grand Canyon

sec.t:
The post office at Hikkim, in the cold desert of [[@spiti|Spiti]] in Himachal Pradesh, stands more than 4,400 metres above sea level. Guinness World Records lists it as the highest in the world, at 4,724 metres, though maps usually put the village a little lower. That is more than half as high as Mount Everest.

Mail from Hikkim goes on foot or by vehicle down to Kaza, the nearest town, then onward by bus. In winter, heavy snow can cut the roads for weeks, and the post office may close. Travellers now come all the way up just to send a postcard with the Hikkim stamp on it.

sec.h: A post office on a boat

sec.t:
A village postal worker does much more than deliver letters. In many places, they also handle savings accounts, pay out old-age pensions, deliver government documents and collect electricity bills. Since 2018, the India Post Payments Bank has let village postal workers carry a small device that works like a bank counter in their bag.

Many walk or cycle long distances. In hilly areas, a single round can mean crossing streams and forest paths. People in the village often know their postal worker by name, and the post office may be the only government office for kilometres around.

Before 1972, Indian letters were sorted by reading the name of the town, which caused confusion, since many towns share names. On 15 August 1972, India introduced the six-digit PIN code, short for Postal Index Number.

The first digit picks one of nine zones (eight regions plus one for the army). The second picks a sub-region, the third a sorting district, and the last three a single post office. A clerk who cannot read a messy address can still send it the right way using the numbers alone.

The United States has its own remote routes. The village of Supai, home of the Havasupai people, sits deep inside a side canyon of the [[@grand-canyon|Grand Canyon]] in Arizona. No road reaches it. The US Postal Service sends mail, groceries and supplies down a trail of about 13 km by mule train, one of the last mule mail routes in the country.

Mail has reached India's Antarctic research bases too. Back in the 1980s, India opened a post office at its first base there, Dakshin Gangotri. The future may be stranger still. India Post has tested [[@drones-delivery|drones]] to fly parcels to hard-to-reach places, cutting journeys that take hours by road to a few minutes in the air.

text: Michael Jackson was called the King of Pop because, in the 1980s, nobody sold more records, filled more stadiums or changed pop music videos as much. His album Thriller (1982) is often called the best-selling album of all time. He sang, wrote songs and danced with moves that millions of children tried to copy in their living rooms.
The nickname stuck after the actress Elizabeth Taylor called him the true king of pop, rock and soul in 1989. His music is still played at weddings, parties and dance classes from Ohio to Odisha.
His life was also troubled, and parts of it remain painful and disputed.

st.reveal: For the video, the dancers were held by wires. For live shows, Jackson and two designers invented shoes with a slot in the heel that caught a peg rising from the stage floor. It held his feet down while he leaned.

d.try: In socks on a smooth floor, try a simple backslide. Keep one foot flat and slide it back while the toes of the other foot press down, then switch. It feels like walking forwards while you glide backwards, the illusion behind the moonwalk.
myth: Michael Jackson invented the moonwalk.

Dancers had performed similar gliding backslides for decades, including Cab Calloway in the 1930s. Jackson made the move world-famous when he performed it on TV in 1983 and gave it the name most people use.

sec.t:
Jackson was born in 1958 in Gary, Indiana, an industrial city in the USA. He was the eighth of ten children. With four of his brothers he formed the Jackson 5, who signed with Motown Records and had four number-one hits in 1969 and 1970.

He was only about 11, but already the lead singer. Later he spoke about how hard his childhood had been, with long hours of rehearsals and a strict father.

As a solo singer, Jackson released Thriller in 1982 with the producer Quincy Jones. Seven of its songs became top-10 hits in the USA. Its sales are usually estimated at more than 60 million copies, though exact totals are hard to check.

Music television had just started. Jackson made videos that were like short films, with stories, costumes and big dance scenes. The "Thriller" video, with dancing zombies, lasted about 14 minutes. At the time, few Black artists were shown on MTV. His videos broke through and helped open the door for others, a small chapter in the long story of [[@civil-rights|civil rights]] in American entertainment. Within a few years, a big-budget music video had become something every pop star wanted.

Jackson toured the world many times. In November 1996 he performed in Mumbai, his only concert in India. Thousands of fans travelled from across the country.

His influence reached Indian films too. The dancer and choreographer Prabhu Deva was often nicknamed "India's Michael Jackson" for his fast, rubbery moves. Many [[@bollywood-dance|Bollywood dances]] of the 1980s and 1990s borrowed his spins, kicks and sharp freezes.

Jackson's appearance changed a lot over the years, and newspapers wrote about his private life constantly. From 1993 he faced serious accusations of harming children. He denied them, and at a trial in 2005 a [[@jury|jury]] found him not guilty. After his death, new accusations were made in a 2019 documentary, and his family and fans disputed them. People still disagree strongly.

He died in Los Angeles in 2009, aged 50, from an overdose of a medicine given by his doctor, who was later convicted. His songs remain among the most played in the world.

text: Yes. Snakes and Ladders comes from India, where it was known by names such as gyan chaupar ("game of knowledge") and moksha patam. Players rolled dice or cowrie shells and moved up a board of squares. Ladders carried them up from squares marked with virtues. Snakes dragged them down from squares marked with vices.

The final square stood for moksha, liberation from the cycle of birth and rebirth. In the late 1800s the game reached Britain, lost its religious meanings and became a family game played around the world.

st.prompt: In traditional Indian versions, what did the ladders stand for?

options.t: Good qualities, like kindness and generosity
Friends who help you on a journey
The steps of a temple

st.reveal: Ladders began on squares for virtues such as faith, generosity and knowledge. Snakes began on squares for vices such as anger, theft and pride. Reaching the top meant reaching moksha, or liberation.

d.try: Design your own Snakes and Ladders board on a sheet of paper with 30 squares. Label each ladder with a good habit, like "shared my lunch", and each snake with a bad one, like "skipped brushing teeth". Play it with a friend using a dice and see who reaches the top.
myth: Snakes and Ladders was invented as a children's game.
In India it began as a game for all ages that taught ideas about karma, good deeds and liberation. It became mainly a children's game after it reached Britain and lost its religious meanings.
facts: gyan chaupar, moksha patam, paramapada sopanam

sec.t:
Nobody knows exactly. Some popular accounts say the 13th-century Marathi saint Dnyaneshwar invented the game, but historians have not found evidence from his time. Most surviving boards were painted in the 1700s and 1800s. Some are now kept in museums such as the Victoria and Albert Museum in London.

The game is related to other Indian race games played on boards, like pachisi. Those are much older, as you can read in [[@board-games|board games]].

British families in India took the game home. By the 1890s it was being sold in Britain as Snakes and Ladders. Board makers cut down the number of squares, usually to 100, and replaced Indian virtues with Victorian ones like obedience and hard work. Later versions dropped the labels entirely.

In 1943 the American company Milton Bradley released Chutes and Ladders, swapping snakes for playground slides. It showed pictures of children doing good deeds at the bottom of ladders and naughty ones at the top of chutes. That is a small echo of the game's Indian roots.

Snakes and Ladders needs no skill at all. Every move depends only on the dice, so a five-year-old has the same chance of winning as a grandmaster. That makes it a favourite with mathematicians who study [[@probability|probability]].

Because each move depends only on the square you are on and the next roll, you can calculate the average length of a game. Mathematicians who studied the classic American board found a single player needs about 39 rolls, on average, to finish. Some games end in fewer than ten. A few, after unlucky snake after snake, seem to go on for ever.

Snakes and Ladders is often a child's first board game. It teaches counting, taking turns and handling the disappointment of sliding down a snake. In India, versions are still sold for festivals such as [[@diwali-lights|Diwali]], and some temples and museums display old gyan chaupar boards.

It is a game where winning says nothing about how clever you are, which is part of its charm. Like [[@cards-games|playing cards]], it travelled the world by changing to suit each place it reached.

text: Ancient people built many clever machines, often using a few simple ideas: the lever, the [[@wheel-invented|wheel]], the pulley, the wedge and the screw. With them they lifted water, moved giant stones, told the time and even predicted [[@eclipses|eclipses]].

The ancient Greeks made [[@gears|gear-driven calculators]] and toy steam engines. Chinese inventors built an earthquake detector and a carriage with a pointer that always faced south. In the Indus Valley, people built covered drains and carefully planned cities over 4,000 years ago. And in India, metalworkers made iron so well that one pillar has hardly rusted in about 1,600 years.

st.reveal: When the ground shook, a weight inside tipped and pushed a ball from one dragon's mouth into a bronze toad's mouth below. The dragon that dropped its ball showed roughly which direction the quake came from.

d.try: Make a simple Archimedes' screw. Wrap a clear plastic tube in a spiral around a bottle, tape it in place, then put the bottom end in a bowl of water with the bottle tilted. Turn the bottle slowly and watch water climb up the spiral and pour out of the top end into a second bowl.
myth: Ancient people were too primitive to build the pyramids and other great monuments by themselves, so they must have had help from aliens.

Archaeologists have found the tools, ramps, quarries, workers' villages and even written records of the people who built the pyramids. Ancient builders were clever engineers using levers, ramps, sledges and huge teams of skilled workers.
facts: about 1,600 years old, from the Gupta period

sec.t:
Moving water was one of the biggest jobs in the ancient world. In Egypt and Mesopotamia, farmers used the shaduf, a long pole with a bucket on one end and a heavy weight on the other. A worker could swing water up from a river with little effort, using the pole as a lever.

The Archimedes' screw, named after the Greek scientist who lived in the 3rd century BCE, is a spiral inside a tube. Turn it, and water climbs up the spiral. Similar screws are still used today to lift water and even move grain. In Persia, engineers dug qanats, [[@extreme-longest-tunnels|long underground tunnels]] that carried water from hills to villages without losing much to evaporation.

How did people build pyramids, temples and huge forts without engines? With levers, ramps, sledges, ropes and lots of organised workers. The Greeks and Romans added cranes powered by [[@pulleys|pulleys]] and giant treadwheels, which workers walked inside like hamsters on a wheel. A Roman treadwheel crane could lift several tonnes.

{{story:wheel-invented}}

Heron of Alexandria, an engineer in Roman Egypt in the 1st century CE, wrote about many inventions. His aeolipile was a hollow metal ball that spun when steam shot out of two bent pipes, an early [[@steam-engine|steam engine]], though it was treated as a curiosity. He also described a machine for temples that gave out a measure of holy water when someone dropped in a coin, often called the first vending machine.

Heron designed automatic theatre shows, with tiny figures moved by falling weights and strings, and temple doors that opened by themselves when a fire was lit on the altar.

In [[@ancient-china|ancient China]], Zhang Heng built a seismoscope in 132 CE: a bronze jar with eight dragons around it, each holding a ball. When an [[@earthquakes|earthquake]] shook the ground, even far away, a ball dropped from one dragon's mouth into a bronze toad's mouth below. The south-pointing chariot used gears so that a figure on top kept pointing the same way, however the chariot turned.

In the Qutb complex in Delhi stands an [[@mystery-iron-pillar|iron pillar]] more than 7 metres tall. It is about 1,600 years old, from the Gupta period, and carries an inscription in Sanskrit. Iron usually [[@rust|rusts]] quickly in rain, but this pillar has stayed almost free of rust.

Scientists, including teams from IIT Kanpur, found that the iron contains a lot of phosphorus. Over time this helped form a thin protective layer on the surface that keeps out water and air. Ancient Indian smiths couldn't have known the chemistry, but their way of making iron worked. Earlier still, the cities of the [[@indus-cities|Indus Valley]] had brick drains running under their streets, something many cities in the world didn't have until the 1800s.

text: A steam engine burns fuel, usually coal or wood, to boil water. When water turns into steam, it takes up well over a thousand times more space, so the steam pushes hard on anything in its way. In an engine, steam pushes a [[piston|piston]], a tight-fitting plug, back and forth inside a metal cylinder. Rods and wheels turn that movement into pumping or turning.

Before steam, almost all work was done by muscles, wind and flowing water. Steam engines could work anywhere, day and night, without getting tired. They pumped mines, drove factory machines, pulled trains and pushed ships, and they helped start the [[@industrial-revolution|Industrial Revolution]].

st.prompt: James Watt's famous improvement in 1769 made steam engines use much less coal. What did he change?

options.t: He cooled the steam in a separate chamber, so the main cylinder could stay hot
He made the engine out of gold, which holds heat better
He added a second chimney

st.reveal: Older engines cooled the steam inside the same cylinder, then had to heat that cylinder up again for every stroke, wasting fuel. Watt's separate condenser meant the cylinder stayed hot all the time, so the same coal did much more work.

d.try: Watch steam push. With an adult in charge of the kitchen, notice how the lid of a pot of boiling water rattles and lifts, or how a pressure cooker whistle jumps. That push comes from water turning into steam, which takes up far more space than the water did. Steam engines harness that same push.
myth: James Watt invented the steam engine.

Working steam engines existed for more than 50 years before Watt's improvement. Thomas Newcomen's engines were pumping water from mines from 1712. Watt made them far more efficient and better at turning wheels, which helped them spread into factories.
facts: Hero of Alexandria, about 2,000 years ago
First steam passenger train in India
in power stations around the world

sec.t:
About 2,000 years ago, [[@ancient-tech|Hero of Alexandria]] was a Greek engineer living in Egypt. He described a metal ball that spun when steam shot out of two bent pipes. It was a clever toy, but nobody used it for work.

The first steam engines with a real job came much later, in England. Coal mines there kept flooding as miners dug deeper. In 1712 Thomas Newcomen built an engine that used steam and the push of the air to work a giant beam, which pumped water up from the mine. It was slow and burned a lot of coal, but at a coal mine, coal was cheap. Some Newcomen engines kept working for decades, nodding their great wooden beams up and down day and night.

Putting a steam engine on wheels created the railway. In 1829, George and Robert Stephenson's locomotive Rocket won a contest in England by pulling a train at what then seemed a shocking speed, close to 50 km/h. Railways soon spread around the globe.

On water, Robert Fulton's steamboat began carrying passengers up the Hudson River from New York in 1807. Ships no longer had to wait for the wind.

In India, the first passenger train ran on 16 April 1853 from Bori Bunder in Bombay to Thane, about 34 km, pulled by three steam locomotives. [[@indian-railways|India's railways]] grew into one of the largest networks anywhere. The little steam engines of the [[@india-wonder-toy-train|Darjeeling Himalayan Railway]], now a [[@unesco-sites|UNESCO World Heritage Site]], still puff up into the hills.

Steam locomotives have mostly retired, but steam itself has not. In most coal, gas and [[@nuclear-power|nuclear]] power stations, heat boils water into high-pressure steam. The steam spins a [[turbine|turbine]], a wheel of angled blades, connected to a generator. Much of the [[@electricity-made|electricity]] in your home was probably made this way.

Burning coal for steam also released huge amounts of carbon dioxide, starting in the 1700s. That is one reason the steam age is part of the story of today's warming climate.

text: Three huge telescopes, much bigger than any working today, are being planned or built. Each has a main mirror between 25 and 39 m wide. For comparison, the biggest telescopes working now have mirrors of about 10 m.

The Extremely Large Telescope, or ELT, is the furthest along. The European Southern Observatory is building it on a mountain in Chile's Atacama Desert. The Giant Magellan Telescope is also planned in Chile. The Thirty Meter Telescope was meant for Hawaii, but its future is uncertain. Astronomers want them to photograph planets around other stars and see the first galaxies.

st.prompt: The Extremely Large Telescope's main mirror is far too big to make in one piece. How many pieces is it made of?
st.reveal: The main mirror is a honeycomb of 798 six-sided segments, each about 1.4 m across. Computers keep them lined up to within a tiny fraction of a hair's width.

d.try: In a dim room, look closely at a friend's eyes, then switch on a bright light and watch their pupils shrink. Your pupil is the opening that lets light in, just like a telescope's mirror. In the dark it opens wide to catch more light, which is exactly why astronomers want bigger mirrors.
myth: Now that we have space telescopes like Webb, big telescopes on the ground are no longer needed.
Ground telescopes can be far bigger than anything we can launch, so they collect much more light. Space and ground telescopes work as a team, each doing jobs the other can't.

sec.t:
A telescope's mirror works like a bucket catching rain, except it catches light. Double the width of the bucket and it catches four times as much. A 39 m mirror gathers far more light than the 6.5 m mirror on the [[@webb-telescope|Webb telescope]].

More light means fainter things become visible. A bigger mirror also shows finer detail. ESO expects the ELT's pictures to be about 15 times sharper than Hubble's. That could be enough to pick out a rocky planet next to a bright star and study the gases in its air.

Stars twinkle because Earth's moving air bends their light. That is pretty, but it blurs telescope pictures. The giant telescopes will use a trick called adaptive optics.

They shine powerful [[@lasers|lasers]] into the sky, which make a glowing dot high in the atmosphere, a kind of artificial star. Sensors watch how the air wobbles that dot. A thin, flexible mirror then bends its shape hundreds of times a second to cancel the wobble. The result can be nearly as sharp as a telescope in space.

Telescopes need high, dry, dark places with steady air. Chile's Atacama Desert is one of the best, which is why it hosts so many observatories.

The Thirty Meter Telescope, or TMT, chose Maunakea, a tall volcano on Hawaii's Big Island. Many Native Hawaiians consider the mountain sacred, and there are already a dozen telescopes on it. In 2019 protesters blocked the road to stop construction. Supporters say the telescope would bring jobs and science. Opponents say the mountain's top has been used enough. A site in Spain's Canary Islands has been studied as a backup. India is one of TMT's partners and is building parts for it, including hardware for its mirror segments.

Giant telescopes take decades and cost billions. As of 2026, the ELT is planned to start observing around 2029. In 2025, the US National Science Foundation moved the Giant Magellan Telescope into its final design stage, but full construction still needs more money. TMT's path is less clear.

All three use the same basic idea as Isaac Newton's first reflecting telescope, built in 1668: a curved [[@mirrors|mirror]] that gathers light to a point. Newton's mirror was a few centimetres wide. The new ones are nearly the width of a building.

text: Tenochtitlan was the capital of the Aztecs, or Mexica, as they called themselves. It stood on an island in Lake Texcoco, high in the Valley of Mexico. In 1519, when Spanish soldiers first saw it, it was probably bigger than any city in Spain.

Three long stone causeways linked it to the shore. Canals ran between the streets, crowded with canoes. At the centre rose a great twin temple painted in bright colours. Gardens floated in the shallows, and fresh water arrived by aqueduct from a hill called Chapultepec. Today the lake has been drained, and Mexico City sits on top of the ruins.

st.prompt: How did people in Tenochtitlan grow food on a city built in a lake?

options.t: On farm plots built up from mud and reeds in the shallow water
On rooftop gardens on every house

st.reveal: The Aztecs built chinampas, long garden plots made from layers of lake mud and plants, held in place by posts and willow trees. Canals between them were used for watering and for canoes. A few still exist at Xochimilco in Mexico City.

n.certNote: Nobody counted Tenochtitlan's people. Historians' estimates range from about 60,000 to more than 200,000, and many settle somewhere between 150,000 and 250,000.

myth: The Aztecs were a small, simple tribe when the Spanish arrived.
The Aztec Empire ruled millions of people across central Mexico. Tenochtitlan had paved causeways, an aqueduct, schools, huge markets and a written system of picture signs.

Fell to Spanish and allied forces

sec.t:
The Mexica told a story about their beginnings. Their god Huitzilopochtli told them to wander until they saw an eagle perched on a cactus. That would be the place for their city. According to tradition, they found it in 1325, on a swampy island nobody else wanted.

It was a poor spot for a city, but a good spot for defence. Over the next two centuries the Mexica turned it into the heart of an empire. The eagle on the cactus is on Mexico's flag today.

North of the main island lay Tlatelolco, a twin city with an enormous market. Hernán Cortés, the Spanish leader, wrote that tens of thousands of people came there every day. Traders sold turkeys, rabbits, cloth, feathers, pottery, gold and medicine. Cacao beans worked as small change, the same beans used to make a frothy, bitter [[@chocolate-making|chocolate]] drink for nobles.

Officials walked through the market checking that measures were fair. Cortés's soldiers, many from Spanish towns of a few thousand people, had never seen anything like it.

The Templo Mayor, or Great Temple, was a stepped pyramid probably more than 40 metres tall, with two shrines on top. One honoured Huitzilopochtli, god of sun and war. The other honoured Tlaloc, god of rain. Ceremonies there included human sacrifice, which the Mexica believed kept the sun moving and the world alive. Historians still debate how many people were killed.

After the Spanish took the city in 1521, they pulled the temple down and built a cathedral nearby. For centuries its exact place was forgotten. Then, in 1978, workers laying electrical cables found a huge round stone carved with the goddess Coyolxauhqui. Archaeologists dug, and the temple's base came to light. You can now walk through the ruins in the middle of the city, a short stroll from the cathedral.

The siege of 1521 destroyed much of Tenochtitlan, and disease had already killed many of its people. The story of how a few hundred Spaniards and many thousands of [[indigenous|Indigenous]] allies brought down the Aztecs is told in the [[@spanish-conquest|Spanish conquest]].

The Spanish drained the lake over the following centuries. Mexico City now sits on soft, old lake mud, and parts of it sink by up to 30 centimetres or more a year as water is pumped from below. Buildings tilt. The ground remembers it was once a lake.

text: Bal Gangadhar Tilak was a teacher, journalist and political leader from Maharashtra. He was one of the first leaders to demand full self-rule for India, which he called *swaraj*, and to take that demand to ordinary people rather than only educated elites. People called him Lokmanya, "the one accepted by the people".

He used newspapers, festivals and fiery speeches to stir up feeling against British rule. The British jailed him more than once. He was also a scholar who wrote about ancient Indian texts. Tilak is admired as a fearless leader. He is also criticised by some historians for opposing certain social reforms of his time.

st.prompt: Tilak helped turn which festival into a big public celebration in the 1890s?

options.t: Ganesh Chaturthi
Diwali
Holi

st.reveal: Families had long worshipped Ganesh at home. From 1893, Tilak encouraged big public celebrations with processions, songs and speeches. They brought people together at a time when British rules limited political meetings.

d.try: Tilak spread his ideas through a newspaper. Make a one-page newspaper about something you think should change at your school or in your street. Give it a name, a headline, one main story and a small drawing. Read it aloud to your family and see whether you persuade them.
myth: Tilak and Gandhi led the freedom movement together.

Tilak was the leading figure before Gandhi. He died on 1 August 1920, the very day Gandhi launched the Non-Cooperation Movement. Their methods also differed, and Tilak was more willing to accept forceful protest.

sec.t:
Tilak was born in 1856 in Ratnagiri, on the Konkan coast, and studied mathematics in [[@pune|Pune]]. With friends, he started schools and the Deccan Education Society, which founded Fergusson College in 1885. They believed Indians should run their own schools and teach patriotism alongside science.

In 1881 he helped launch two weekly [[@newspapers|newspapers]]: *Kesari* in Marathi and *Mahratta* in English. *Kesari* means lion. Its sharp articles attacked British policies, and it reached farmers and shopkeepers who couldn't read English. That reach made Tilak far more powerful than a leader writing only for the educated few.

Inside the Indian National Congress, Tilak led the "extremists", who wanted bold action. The "moderates", led by people like Gopal Krishna Gokhale, preferred petitions and slow reform. Tilak, Lala Lajpat Rai and Bipin Chandra Pal became known together as Lal-Bal-Pal.

When the British split Bengal in 1905, Tilak backed the protests that followed the [[@bengal-partition-1905|partition of Bengal]]. He urged people to boycott British goods and buy Indian ones. His slogan, "Swaraj is my birthright, and I shall have it", spread across the country and became one of the movement's most repeated lines.

In 1908, Tilak was tried for sedition, meaning stirring up rebellion, because of articles in *Kesari*. He was sent to prison in Mandalay, in Burma, for six years. Far from home, often unwell, he read widely and wrote *Gita Rahasya*, a long study of the [[@bhagavad-gita|Bhagavad Gita]]. He argued that the Gita teaches people to act and do their duty, rather than to withdraw from the world.

He returned in 1914 and soon helped start a Home Rule League to push for self-government. Annie Besant set up a similar league at about the same time, and the two campaigns sent speakers into towns and villages across India. In 1916, Tilak also helped bring about the Lucknow Pact, an agreement between the Congress and the Muslim League to press the British together.

Tilak was a social conservative in some ways. In 1891, he opposed a British law raising the age at which girls could be married. He argued that Indians, not British rulers, should reform Indian customs. Critics then and now say this slowed down changes that would have protected girls.

Tilak died in Bombay on 1 August 1920. That same day, Gandhi launched the [[@non-cooperation|Non-Cooperation Movement]], and the leadership of the struggle passed to him. Huge crowds followed Tilak's funeral procession. Gandhi later called him "the maker of modern India".

text: Khajuraho is a small town in [[@madhya-pradesh|Madhya Pradesh]] with one of the finest groups of medieval temples in India. They were built between about 950 and 1050 CE by the Chandela kings, who ruled this part of central India.

Most are Hindu temples to Shiva and Vishnu, but a cluster of them belongs to the [[@mahavira|Jain]] faith. Nearly every outside wall is covered in carvings: gods, heavenly dancers, musicians, elephants, warriors and ordinary people going about their day. In 1986 the temples became a [[@unesco-sites|UNESCO World Heritage Site]].

options.t: About 25
All 85
Just 2

st.reveal: About 25 temples survive, spread over roughly 6 square kilometres. The rest crumbled, were taken apart for building stone or lie as mounds of rubble that archaeologists still study.

d.try: Build a temple tower from boxes or cups. Put the biggest at the bottom and stack smaller ones on top, then crowd little "peaks" around the main one so the whole thing rises like a mountain range. That is how a Khajuraho tower is meant to look, a stone copy of the Himalaya.
myth: The Khajuraho temples are mostly covered in carvings of couples.
Only a small share of the carvings show couples. Most show gods and goddesses, musicians, dancers, soldiers, animals and scenes of daily life such as women writing letters or putting on make-up.

sec.t:
Walk around Kandariya Mahadeva and you pass hundreds of figures, some no taller than your arm. Many are *apsaras*, heavenly women caught in the middle of a movement: one pulls a thorn from her foot, one looks into a mirror, one writes a letter. Sculptors carved them with bent hips and turned heads, so the stone seems to sway.

Elephants, horses and soldiers march along the lower bands. Higher up are gods and their attendants. A small share of the [[@temple-sculpture|carvings]] show couples, and these get most of the attention from tourists. Historians have different ideas about why they are there. Some link them to Tantric beliefs, some to ideas about life's four goals, and others think they were simply part of showing the whole of human life.

The temples are usually split into three groups. The western group is the largest and holds the most famous Hindu temples, including Kandariya Mahadeva and the Lakshmana temple, one of the earliest, finished around 954 CE.

The eastern group includes the Jain temples. The biggest, the Parshvanath temple, has some of the most delicate carving on the whole site, and Jain pilgrims still worship there today. A short drive south, the southern group has a couple of later temples standing alone among fields.

Hindu and Jain temples were built side by side, by the same kinds of craftsmen, during the same years. The Chandela kings were Hindu, but rich Jain merchants in their kingdom paid for temples of their own, and the two styles look like close cousins.

After the Chandela kingdom faded in the 1200s and 1300s, Khajuraho stopped being a royal centre. Local people still worshipped at some temples, but the forest grew back around the others.

In 1838 a British army engineer, T. S. Burt, was taken to the site by local guides and wrote about what he saw. Later the Archaeological Survey of India cleared the plants, repaired the platforms and began protecting the temples. The name is usually explained by the word *khajur*, the date palm, which once grew here.

Every February since the 1970s, the Khajuraho Dance Festival has brought performers of Kathak, Bharatanatyam, Odissi and other forms of [[@indian-classical-dance|classical dance]] to an open-air stage in front of the western temples. Some of the poses the dancers strike can be found, a thousand years older, on the walls just behind them.

Today the town has a small airport and a railway station, and visitors from around the world come to walk the stone platforms at sunrise, when the sandstone turns gold.

text: Uttarakhand is a Himalayan state in northern India, and many Hindus call it Dev Bhoomi, the land of the gods. Some of Hinduism's holiest rivers rise here, and its mountains hold ancient temples that pilgrims have visited for centuries. The four shrines of the Char Dham, at Yamunotri, Gangotri, Kedarnath and Badrinath, sit high in the valleys.

The name fits the land as well as the faith. Snowy peaks such as Nanda Devi, at about 7,800 m one of India's highest mountains, rise above deep river gorges and thick forests. The state was formed in 2000, when it was separated from Uttar Pradesh, and its capital is Dehradun.

st.prompt: The river Ganga gets its name at a town called Devprayag. What happens there?

A glacier melts into a waterfall
The river flows out of a cave

st.reveal: Above Devprayag the two rivers have different names. The Bhagirathi comes from the Gangotri glacier and the Alaknanda from near Badrinath. From the point where they meet, the river is called the Ganga.

myth: The Ganga flows straight out of a single spring at Gangotri.

Its main source stream, the Bhagirathi, comes out of a glacier at Gaumukh, about 18 km above Gangotri town. Many other streams and rivers, including the Alaknanda, join before the river is called the Ganga.

sec.t:
The Yamuna starts near the Yamunotri shrine. The Bhagirathi, the main source stream of the Ganga, pours out of the Gangotri [[@glaciers|glacier]] at a spot called Gaumukh, the "cow's mouth". Another river, the Alaknanda, flows down from near Badrinath.

At Devprayag, the Bhagirathi and the Alaknanda meet, one greenish and one greyer, and from there the river is called the Ganga. It reaches the plains at Haridwar, where millions gather for the Kumbh Mela, and flows on past cities like [[@varanasi|Varanasi]] to the sea.

In the 1970s, villagers in the Garhwal hills grew angry as contractors [[@what-if-no-trees|cut down forests]] the villagers depended on for firewood, fodder and water. In 1974, in the village of Reni, a group of women led by Gaura Devi stood between the loggers and the trees and refused to move.

Their protest became part of the Chipko movement, from a Hindi word meaning "to stick" or "to hug". It inspired environmental campaigns across India and beyond, and helped lead to limits on felling trees in the Himalaya. The idea of standing up for a forest by hugging its trees spread to villages in Karnataka and elsewhere.

In 1936, the British set up India's first national park in the foothills. It was later renamed after [[@kipling-india|Jim Corbett]], a hunter who became a conservationist and wrote books about the region. Today, Jim Corbett National Park is one of the best places in India to see a tiger in the wild.

Higher up, the [[@india-wonder-valley-flowers|Valley of Flowers]] bursts into bloom each monsoon, with hundreds of kinds of wildflowers. Together with nearby Nanda Devi National Park, it is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The mountains can be dangerous, though. In 2013, sudden floods swept through the Kedarnath valley, causing great loss of life. Scientists continue to study how heavy rain, melting ice and building on steep slopes can combine to cause such disasters.

text: Great adventure books take ordinary people into danger and make them find out what they're made of. There might be a shipwreck, a hunt for treasure, a race across the world or a night alone in the woods. You keep turning pages because you need to know what happens next.

Some classics have been read for centuries, like Robinson Crusoe (1719) and Treasure Island (1883). Others are newer favourites, like Hatchet (1987). India has its own heroes too, from [[@satyajit-ray-stories|Satyajit Ray]]'s detective Feluda to the boys and girls of [[@ruskin-bond|Ruskin Bond]]'s mountain stories. Here are some of the best, and why they still work.

He found a real pirate's diary in an old house
A newspaper paid him to write about a real treasure hunt

st.reveal: In 1881, on a wet holiday in Scotland, Stevenson painted a map of an island with his stepson Lloyd. Looking at it, he began imagining the pirates who buried treasure there, and he read each new chapter aloud to the family.

myth: Real pirates buried their treasure and drew maps with an X to mark the spot.
Real pirates almost never buried treasure. They usually spent or shared it quickly. Buried chests, X-marked maps and parrots on shoulders were made famous by Treasure Island and later films.

sec.t:
Daniel Defoe's Robinson Crusoe came out in 1719. A sailor is shipwrecked on an island and survives alone for years, building a shelter, growing crops and keeping a diary. It was one of the first English novels, and it started a craze for castaway stories.

Island of the Blue Dolphins (1960), by the American writer Scott O'Dell, is based on a real Native American woman. She lived alone on San Nicolas Island, off California, for about 18 years in the 1800s. In the book, a girl named Karana builds a home, tames a wild dog and survives by her own skill.

In [[@jules-verne|Jules Verne]]'s Around the World in Eighty Days (1872), the very precise Englishman Phileas Fogg bets that he can circle the globe in 80 days. His journey includes a train across India and a ride on an elephant when the railway line runs out. Verne made travel itself the adventure.

Mark Twain's The Adventures of Tom Sawyer (1876) brought adventure closer to home: caves, a haunted house and a raft on the Mississippi River.

In Gary Paulsen's Hatchet, 13-year-old Brian Robeson is the only survivor when a small plane crashes in the Canadian wilderness. He has nothing but a hatchet his mother gave him. He learns to make fire, catch fish and survive a moose attack.

Paulsen knew wild country first-hand. He trapped, hunted and ran the Iditarod sled-dog race across Alaska twice. Hatchet was named a Newbery Honor Book in 1988.

In 1965, Satyajit Ray published the first story about Feluda, a sharp-eyed private detective from Kolkata, in the children's magazine Sandesh. With his young cousin Topshe narrating, Feluda solves mysteries in places like Rajasthan, Varanasi and Sikkim. Many stories are as much travel adventures as crime puzzles.

Ruskin Bond wrote many short adventure stories set in the hills and forests of north India. In Angry River, a girl named Sita is swept away when floods rise around her island home. [[@jungle-book|The Jungle Book]] by Rudyard Kipling, set in the forests of central India, has kept children reading since 1894.

Adventure books share a few tricks. The hero is usually young or ordinary, so you can picture yourself in their place. There's a clear goal and a clock ticking. And the hero has to solve problems with their own wits and [[@courage|courage]].

They also teach you things without seeming to. After Hatchet, many readers know how to make a fire with a spark. After Around the World in Eighty Days, they know how the date line works. A good adventure leaves you feeling as if you went too.

text: Sukumar Ray was a Bengali poet, writer and illustrator who lived from 1887 to 1923. He is best known for *Abol Tabol*, a book of nonsense poems full of strange creatures, odd characters and invented words. For over a century, Bengali children have [[@poems-for-kids|learned these poems by heart]], often before they can read.

Ray is often compared to Britain's Edward Lear and [[@alice-wonderland|Lewis Carroll]], who also wrote nonsense. Like them, he made up words that sound like they ought to mean something, and he drew his own pictures. He died young, at 35, but his rhymes are still recited at school functions and quoted by grown-ups across Bengal.

st.prompt: In his poem "Khichuri", Sukumar Ray joins a duck (*hansh*) and a porcupine (*sajaru*). What does he call the new animal?

Duckupine
Sajarhansh

st.reveal: He squashes the two names together into *hanshjaru*, a "mixed-up" creature, just as the poem's name, Khichuri, is a dish of mixed rice and dal. A heron and a tortoise get the same treatment and become *bakachhap*.

sec.t:
Ray was born in [[@kolkata|Calcutta]], into a family of writers, artists and printers. His father, Upendrakishore Ray Chowdhury, wrote children's stories, played the violin, studied astronomy and ran a printing business. He was one of the first in India to experiment with halftone printing, a way of printing photos and shaded pictures using tiny dots.

Sukumar studied physics and chemistry, then went to England from 1911 to 1913 to learn the latest printing technology. When he returned, he joined the family business.

In 1913, his father started a [[@childrens-magazines|children's magazine]] called *Sandesh*. After Upendrakishore died in 1915, Sukumar took it over. He filled its pages with his own poems, stories, drawings and articles.

{{story:printing-revolution}}

sec.h: Ducks, porcupines and a crying cat
sec.t:
*Abol Tabol*, roughly "gibberish" or "topsy-turvy", collects his best-known poems. In "Khichuri", animals get mashed together: a duck and porcupine become a *hanshjaru*, a heron and tortoise a *bakachhap*.

Other poems introduce a man who wears his moustache as a sign of dignity and panics when he thinks it has been stolen, and a kingdom run by twenty-one ridiculous laws. Ray drew the pictures for the book himself, in pen and ink, and his creatures look every bit as odd as they sound. The rhythm makes them fun to chant aloud, and the jokes often have a sting. Officials, know-it-alls and stuffy rules are frequent targets.

He also wrote *HaJaBaRaLa*, a prose story in which a boy dozes off on a hot afternoon. His handkerchief turns into a cat, a crow does strange sums, and he ends up in a very odd courtroom. It is often compared to *Alice in Wonderland*.

In 1921, Sukumar's only son, Satyajit, was born. Soon after, Sukumar fell ill with kala-azar, a disease spread by the bite of sandflies. There was no good cure then. He kept writing and drawing in bed, and prepared *Abol Tabol* for print. He died in September 1923, and the book was published days later.

*Sandesh* faded after his death. Decades later, in 1961, [[@satyajit-ray|Satyajit Ray]], by then a world-famous film-maker, revived the magazine and wrote his own detective and science stories for it. In 1987 he made a documentary film about his father.

Nonsense is hard to translate, because so much of it depends on sound. Even so, Ray's poems have been translated into English, most famously by Sukanta Chaudhuri, and into other Indian languages.

Readers who enjoy [[@dr-seuss|Dr. Seuss]] in the USA often find a kindred spirit in Sukumar Ray. Both played with rhythm, invented words and drew odd creatures. Ray did it more than a decade before Dr. Seuss published his first children's book, in Bengali, for a magazine read by children in Calcutta.

text: Chillies are from the Americas. People in what is now Mexico were growing them more than 6,000 years ago. When Christopher [[@columbus|Columbus]] reached the Caribbean in 1492, he tasted them and took them back to Spain.

Within a few decades, Portuguese ships carried chillies around Africa to their trading base in Goa, on India's west coast. The plant grew easily in Indian soil and was cheap to grow. In less than a century, it had spread across the country and changed Indian cooking for good.

st.prompt: Chillies taste painfully hot to mammals. Why might a chilli plant gain from that?

options.t: Mammals avoid eating the fruit, leaving it for birds, which spread the seeds better
The heat keeps the plant warm at night
It helps the fruit ripen faster in the sun

st.reveal: Mammals tend to crush seeds with their teeth. Birds swallow chilli seeds whole and drop them far away, unharmed. Since birds can't feel capsaicin, the burn works like a lock that only the right animals can open.

myth: The seeds are the hottest part of a chilli.
Most of the capsaicin is made in the pale, spongy ribs inside the chilli, which hold the seeds. Seeds taste hot because they touch those ribs.

sec.t:
Indian food was spicy long before chillies arrived. The heat came from [[@cardamom-pepper|black pepper]], long pepper (called pippali), ginger and [[@mustard|mustard]]. Pepper was expensive, though, because so much of it was sold abroad.

So when Europeans saw this new fruit, they called it a "pepper" too, because it burned the tongue. That is why chillies are still called peppers in the USA and Britain, even though they belong to a completely different plant family. In several Indian languages the chilli's name borrowed from the word for pepper: in [[@hindi-language|Hindi]], *kali mirch* is black pepper and *lal mirch* is [[@food-why-chillies-red|red chilli]].

The heat of a chilli comes from a chemical called [[capsaicin|capsaicin]]. It doesn't actually burn you. It fits into the same sensors in your mouth that detect real heat, so your brain gets a false fire alarm.

In 1912, an American chemist named Wilbur Scoville invented a test to measure chilli heat. Tasters sipped chilli extract mixed with more and more sugar water until they could no longer feel the burn. The Scoville scale is still used, though labs now measure [[@food-science-spicy-milk|capsaicin]] with machines.

In 2007, a chilli from [[@northeast-india|Northeast India]] called bhut jolokia, or ghost pepper, was named the hottest chilli in the world by [[@world-records|Guinness World Records]]. It is grown in Assam, Nagaland and Manipur, and is hundreds of times hotter than a typical green chilli. Newer hybrids bred in the USA have since beaten it.

Not every Indian chilli is fiery. Kashmiri chillies are mild and give [[@kashmiri-wazwan|rogan josh]] its deep red colour. Byadgi chillies from Karnataka are prized for colour too. Many cooks use one kind for heat and another for colour in the same dish.

Chillies are still at the heart of Mexican cooking, from mild poblanos to smoky chipotles. [[@thailand|Thai]], Korean and Sichuan Chinese food, all famous for their heat, also got their chillies after 1500. In just 500 years, a plant from one corner of the world became the most widely grown spice on Earth.
